Stage 3 · Reading

The families we did not have

Everyone knows what their brothers and sisters did to them. Twenty thousand people suggest otherwise.

👪💭
1 · Before you read. How much do you think your position in the family shaped your character?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

The families we did not have

Written for this course. The four speakers are composites, not interviews. Research from Rohrer, Egloff & Schmukle, PNAS 112(46), 2015, and Falbo & Polit, Psychological Bulletin 100(2), 1986.

1Ask people about family size and you will hear principles. Ask them about their own childhood and you will hear something more useful. Here are four familiar kinds of answer, and one problem with all of them.

2The only child says she was never spoilt, which everybody with a sibling assumes she was, and that her godparent took her more seriously than either grandmother did, as did a second cousin she still writes to. If she had had a brother, she says, she would have learnt earlier how to stand up to bullies; as it was, she learnt it at twenty-three, in an office. She would not change it. She would simply have liked one person to be mean to her at the right age.

3The third of four describes years of feeling left out and mentions it once, in passing, as though it were a weather report. His older brother told him off more often than his parents ever did. If his mother had not become ill, he thinks, he would still not be speaking to that brother; somebody had to care for her, they both moved home, and the relationship changed in a single winter. He is now devoted to a brother he did not speak to for six years. The mother of four calls it a blessing and a travelling circus, and says the joy each one brings is immeasurable and the strain enormous.

4The fourth speaker, who has no children, is the one who spots the pattern: everybody defends the family they have. If she had had children, she says, she would be defending them now, and she would be just as certain as everyone else in the room, and she would have no more evidence than they do.

5She is closer to the research than the others. In 2015 three psychologists combined data from three national panels — more than twenty thousand adults in Germany, the United States and Britain — to test the oldest folk theory in the field. They confirmed one small effect: firstborns score slightly higher on measured intelligence, and rate their own intellect slightly higher too. On personality they found nothing. No birth-order effect on how outgoing people were, how emotionally stable, how agreeable, how conscientious, how imaginative. The differences everybody can describe from their own kitchen did not appear in twenty thousand people.

6The only child fares no worse. A review of the research had already concluded that only children do as well as anybody else, and better on some measures, which will disappoint several centuries of confident opinion about them. What all this leaves is a strange situation. The sentences people use about their families are almost all counterfactual — if I had had a sister, if he had not been born first — and a counterfactual cannot be checked, because the other family was never run. That is not a reason to stop saying them. It is a reason to notice that they describe a feeling accurately and a cause not at all.

Text A · Four familiar answers

Written for this course. The four speakers are composites, not interviews.

Ask people about family size and you will hear principles. Ask them about their own childhood and you will hear something more useful. Here are four familiar kinds of answer, and one problem with all of them.

The only child says she was never spoilt, which everybody with a sibling assumes she was, and that her godparent took her more seriously than either grandmother did, as did a second cousin she still writes to. If she had had a brother, she says, she would have learnt earlier how to stand up to bullies; as it was, she learnt it at twenty-three, in an office. She would not change it. She would simply have liked one person to be mean to her at the right age.

The third of four describes years of feeling left out and mentions it once, in passing, as though it were a weather report. His older brother told him off more often than his parents ever did. If his mother had not become ill, he thinks, he would still not be speaking to that brother; somebody had to care for her, they both moved home, and the relationship changed in a single winter. He is now devoted to a brother he did not speak to for six years. The mother of four calls it a blessing and a travelling circus, and says the joy each one brings is immeasurable and the strain enormous. The fourth speaker, who has no children, is the one who spots the pattern: everybody defends the family they have. If she had had children, she says, she would be defending them now, and she would be just as certain as everyone else in the room, and she would have no more evidence than they do.

Text B · Twenty thousand adults

Written for this course, from Rohrer, Egloff & Schmukle, PNAS 112(46), 2015, and Falbo & Polit, Psychological Bulletin 100(2), 1986.

The fourth speaker is closer to the research than the others. In 2015 three psychologists combined data from three national panels — more than twenty thousand adults in Germany, the United States and Britain — to test the oldest folk theory in the field: that your position among your brothers and sisters shapes the person you become. They confirmed one small effect. Firstborns score slightly higher on measured intelligence, and rate their own intellect slightly higher too. If the effect had been any larger, somebody would have found it decades ago.

On personality they found nothing. No birth-order effect on how outgoing people were, how emotionally stable, how agreeable, how conscientious, how imaginative. The differences everybody can describe from their own kitchen, in detail, with examples, did not appear in twenty thousand people. The only child fares no worse either: a review of the research had already concluded that only children do as well as anybody else, and better on some measures, which will disappoint several centuries of confident opinion about them. If the study had confirmed what everybody expected, it would have been reported everywhere; as it was, the null result had to be argued for.

What all this leaves is a strange situation. The sentences people use about their families are almost all counterfactual — if I had had a sister, if he had not been born first, if she had not been the youngest — and a counterfactual cannot be checked, because the other family was never run. Nobody grew up twice. That is not a reason to stop saying them, and the four speakers are not being foolish. It is a reason to notice that such a sentence describes a feeling accurately and a cause not at all.

Stage 4 · Unreal situations

Second conditional, third conditional, and the mixture

Two patterns for things that are not true, and one for a past that did not happen still shaping a present that did.

One rule holds across all of them: no would in the if clause. If she would have had a brother is the single most common error at this level, and it is always wrong.

4 · One family, six unreal sentences.
If I had a sister, I would ask her.  →  unreal now.
If I had had a sister, I would have asked her.  →  unreal past.
If I had had a sister, I would not be alone now.  →  past cause, present result.
If I were more patient, I would not have said it.  →  permanent fact, past result.
If I had asked, she might have told me.  →  possibility, not certainty.
Had I known, I would have called.  →  formal inversion.
1 · Read the explanation.
Talking about what is not true

Unreal now: the second conditional. If + past simple, then would + verb. The past tense does not mean past time; it marks the whole sentence as untrue. If I had a sister, I would ask her — I have no sister.

Unreal past: the third conditional. If + past perfect, then would have + past participle. Both halves are the opposite of what happened. If she had had a brother, she would have learnt earlier — she had none, and she did not.

Mixed, past to present. A past condition with a result you can see now: if + past perfect, would + verb. If his mother had not become ill, he would still not be speaking to his brother.

Mixed, present to past. A permanent fact with a past result: if + past simple, would have + participle. If he were more patient, he would not have said it.

Other modals. Would is certainty; could is ability; might is possibility. If I had asked, she might have told me is more honest than would have told me in most real cases.

Were and inversion. Use were for all persons in unreal sentences: if I were, if he were. In formal writing, if can be dropped and the auxiliary moved to the front: Had I known, Were I you.

The unbreakable rule. No would after if. Not if she would have had; not if I would be.

The commonest errors at this level
  • If she would have had a brother… — never would in the if clause.
  • If I would be you… — If I were you.
  • If she had had a brother, she would learn — the halves do not match.
  • If he was more patient in formal writing — use were.
  • Using would have for a present result that is still true.

Two things to watch

1 — Ask when the result is. If the result is visible today, the second half is would + verb, even when the condition is past.

2 — The tense is a marker, not a time. Had in if I had a sister is not the past; it is the sign that the sentence is untrue.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Building an unreal sentence step by step

The facts: his mother became ill; the brothers had to share her care; they are speaking to each other again now.

Step 1 — reverse the condition. The real cause was the illness, so the unreal version is if his mother had not become ill — past perfect, because it did happen.

Step 2 — decide when the result is. Not speaking to each other is the situation now, so the second half is would + verb, not would have.

Step 3 — reverse the result too. They are speaking now, so the unreal version is he would still not be speaking to him.

Step 4 — check the if clause. No would anywhere near it. The finished sentence: If his mother had not become ill, he would still not be speaking to his brother.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Two patterns, and two mixtures

Second conditional — if + past simple, would + verb — unreal now or in general: If I had a sister, I would ask her. I have no sister.

Third conditional — if + past perfect, would have + participle — unreal in the past: If she had had a brother, she would have learnt to argue. She had none, and she did not learn.

Mixed, past → now — if + past perfect, would + verb: a past cause with a present result: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now. Mixed, now → past — if + past simple, would have + participle: a permanent fact with a past result: If he were more patient, he would not have said it.

The rule behind all four: the if-clause takes the tense of the cause, and the main clause the tense of the result. Once you see that, the mixtures stop being exceptions.

were, other modals, and inversion

Were rather than was is standard in unreal sentences for every person: If I were you · if he were more patient. Was is heard in speech and is not wrong there, but If I were you is fixed and never varies.

Could and might replace would when you mean ability or possibility rather than certainty: If we had left earlier, we could have caught it (we would have been able to) · If I had asked, she might have told me (perhaps). Using would have for all three claims more than you know.

Inversion replaces if in formal writing, and the auxiliary moves to the front: Had she had a brother, she would have learnt · Were I in your position, I would refuse. Note that there is no if at all in these sentences; Had if she known is wrong.

Errors to watch: If I would have a sister → if I had — would never goes in the if-clause · If she would have had a brother → if she had had · If I had studied medicine, I would have been a doctor now → would be, because the result is now · Had if I known → Had I known.

1 · Read the model.
Model · four paragraphs

I grew up as the oldest of two, with four years between us, in a flat where the second bedroom was the size of a cupboard. The fact I want to change is the four years. If we had been eighteen months apart, almost everything about that flat would have been different.

We would have fought, for one thing. As it was, I was told off for things she did and never resented it, because at nine you cannot resent a five-year-old; at seven and eight we would have been equals, and equals argue. I would probably have been meaner to her and less devoted, and she would not have looked up to me for as long as she did. I would also have learnt to stand up to people earlier, which I did not learn until university, and which cost me two years there.

The present would be different too. If we had grown up as near-equals, I do not think I would be the one who cares for our parents now; that job went to me because I was always the older one, and it has never been discussed. She would probably live closer. Our relationship might be warmer, or it might not exist at all, and I genuinely cannot tell which.

One thing would be the same. We both take after our father in the way we avoid a difficult conversation, and no arrangement of birthdays would have fixed that. Whatever the gap had been, we would still be two people who send each other articles instead of asking how the other one is.
